title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
This is the closing page of a fragment from the Adversaria mathematica (A.m. T. I, pp. 37–41). Its main object is an integrability ('sine integratione') construction. We have only the end, so the geometry is not fully recoverable. It involves angles x, y, ω, ξ, φ and a slope angle r with tan r = dq/dp, all expressed through two auxiliary quantities p, q. The preceding page sets up the following.
(i) A relation sin ω = √(1−p²−q²)/sin y, with cos y = q cos r − p sin r, which looks like a spherical-trigonometry relation.
(ii) A trial integral −cot ξ = −u cot r + t, with u and t required not to depend on r. This gives dφ = (du cot r − dt) sin²ξ.
(iii) Since u and t are free of r, the defining identity must hold for r = 0 and r = 90°. This gives u = (1−q²)/√(1−p²−q²) and, from the quadratic, t = −pq/√(1−p²−q²).

On this page:
1. cot ξ = ((1−q²)cot r + pq)/√D, with D = 1−p²−q².
2. Hence sin²ξ = D/[(1−q²)((1−p²) + 2pq cot r + (1−q²)cot²r)]. This uses the identity D + p²q² = (1−p²)(1−q²).
3. Using dp = dq·cot r, the previous page gives du cot r − dt = p dq[(1−q²)cot²r + 2pq cot r + (1−p²)]/D^{3/2}.
4. The bracket cancels against sin²ξ, leaving dφ = p dq/((1−q²)√D). The slope r, and with it dp, drop out.

Euler then turns this into a solution of the problem in terms of an arbitrary function, with no quadrature:
- Choose any algebraic relation between sin φ and q, and set s = dφ/dq (an algebraic quantity).
- Solve √(1−p²−q²) = p/(s(1−q²)) for p. Explicitly p² = s²(1−q²)³/(1 + s²(1−q²)²); Euler leaves this implicit.
- Then tan r = dq/dp, u = (1−q²)/√D, t = −pq/√D = −sq(1−q²).
- Then cos y = q cos r − p sin r, cot ξ = u cot r − t, and x = ξ + φ.

In modern terms this is an explicit, integration-free parametrisation of all solutions of an underdetermined differential relation by one arbitrary function. That is what is now called a Monge-type or 'differentially flat' parametrisation.

The NB asks for an a-priori criterion for cot r to cancel in dφ = (du cot r − dt)/(u²cot²r − 2tu cot r + 1 + t²). Euler tries to eliminate p in favour of t and u:
- He obtains u√D = 1−q², (1+t²)√D = u(1−p²) and p² = 1 − (1+t²)(1−q²)/u².
- This leads to the biquadratic q⁴ − q²(1−t²−u²) = t².
- He concludes it is better to keep p and q as variables, because then dp = dq cot r reveals the cancellation at once.

Finally he notes dφ = −t dq/(q(1−q²)), so t = −sq(1−q²).
errors: Previous page, final displayed line: the factor should read p dq((1−qq)cot²r + 2pq cot r + (1−pp))/(1−pp−qq)^{3/2}. As transcribed it has an extra factor p inside each term ('p cot²r(1−qq) … + p(1−pp)'). The preceding line and this page's result dφ = p dq/((1−qq)√(1−pp−qq)) confirm the corrected form. It is a typo or transcription slip, not a mathematical error.

On this page every step checks out: sin²ξ, the cancellation giving dφ, the formula t = −sq(1−qq), and the biquadratic q⁴ − qq(1−tt−uu) = tt. The NB criterion is not actually supplied in general; Euler only remarks that it is evident in the p,q variables. That is a gap he acknowledges himself.

ideas.what: Choose an ansatz cot ξ = u cot r − t with u, t independent of the slope angle r, and fix u and t by specialising r = 0 and r = 90°.
ideas.modern_name: Undetermined-coefficient ansatz / separation in the slope parameter (Legendre-type use of the tangent angle as a variable)
ideas.where_published: Similar devices appear in Euler's papers on algebraic or rectifiable curves; exact parallel unsure

ideas.what: Integration-free complete solution: an arbitrary algebraic relation between sin φ and q determines all the other quantities algebraically, with r eliminated via tan r = dq/dp.
ideas.modern_name: Explicit parametrisation of an underdetermined ODE by an arbitrary function (Monge problem; differential flatness)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Monge (1784), Hilbert (1912), Cartan (1914); flatness: Fliess–Lévine–Martin–Rouchon (1990s). Euler used such methods for algebraically rectifiable curves.
ideas.where_published: Euler's papers on algebraic rectifiable curves (plane and spherical) use the same philosophy; this specific spherical problem possibly only in the Adversaria / Opera postuma

ideas.what: Reduction of the cancellation criterion to a biquadratic q⁴ − q²(1−t²−u²) = t² linking the old and new variables.

missed.claim: Euler explicitly asks for an a-priori criterion for when the slope cot r drops out of dφ = (du cot r − dt) sin²ξ. Such a criterion would explain when the 'method without integration' works. He leaves it open, observing only that it is visible in the p,q variables. In modern terms this asks when the system is flat, or linearisable by an algebraic contact transformation.
missed.quote: Hic autem etiamnunc desideratur criterium, ex quo pateat in formula dφ=(du cot r − dt) sin²ξ quantitatem cot r ex calculo tolli; in hoc ipso enim vis methodi consistit
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is an early statement of the problem of characterising differentially flat / Monge-parametrisable systems. Histories of flatness usually start with Monge and Hilbert, and this could be a small pre-Monge data point.

missed.claim: The final recipe is an explicit, quadrature-free, one-arbitrary-function parametrisation of solutions, here in a spherical-trigonometric setting. It is the same structure as Monge/Hilbert parametrisations, a link rarely credited to Euler's Adversaria.
missed.quote: Constituta relatione quacunque algebraica inter sin φ et q, positoque dφ/dq = s, quaeratur quantitas p
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical precedence for flatness-type parametrisations; minor.

deep.surprise_reason: The algebra is correct and largely routine. The page does contain a clear statement of an open 'criterion' problem, essentially when a slope variable can be eliminated so the solution is algebraically parametrised. That anticipates Monge/Hilbert flatness questions. However, Euler's general method of solving without integration is known, and the underlying geometric problem cannot be identified from this page alone.

Page header reads 'Calc. integr.' (truncated in the scan as 'Calc. integ…').
Step 2: t = −pq/√(1−pp−qq) = −sq(1−qq) — the scan shows '(1−qq)' with a smudge on the 1; reading is correct.
